nameStory: Black henbane gets its ominous name from its deadly effect on chickens and other poultry - 'hen' plus 'bane' meaning poison or death. The 'black' part refers to the dark seeds hidden within its innocent-looking flowers. It's also called 'stinking nightshade' because of its unpleasant, fetid odor that warns of its toxic nature.
description: Black henbane is a highly poisonous annual or biennial herb in the nightshade family, standing 1-3 feet tall. This European native has sticky, hairy leaves and produces funnel-shaped flowers that are pale yellow with dark purple veins running through them like roadmaps. The entire plant has an unpleasant, rank smell that's hard to forget once you've encountered it. Though rare in New England with only one recorded observation, it's important to recognize due to its extreme toxicity.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Funnel-shaped flowers are pale yellow or cream-colored with distinctive dark purple or brownish veins creating a spidery network pattern across the petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, oval leaves feel sticky and clammy to the touch due to dense, glandular hairs that also give off a strong, unpleasant odor when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a robust, somewhat sprawling plant 1-3 feet tall with thick, branching stems covered in sticky hairs

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces urn-shaped seed capsules with a lid that opens to reveal numerous small, dark seeds nestled inside like tiny black beads

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Entire plant emits a strong, fetid odor described as musty, rank, or like rotting vegetation - particularly noticeable when leaves are disturbed

habitat: In New England, black henbane is extremely rare and typically found in disturbed soils near human habitation, such as waste areas, roadsides, or old farmsteads. It prefers rich, well-drained soils and often appears in areas where European settlers once lived, as it likely arrived with early colonists.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic sticky, foul-smelling leaves forming a basal rosette close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when the distinctive yellow flowers with purple veins are most visible and the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing dark seeds while leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil; biennial plants may persist as low rosettes.

funFact: Black henbane contains the same psychoactive compounds found in witch's flying ointments from medieval times - it was literally one of the secret ingredients that gave people hallucinations of flight, explaining some historical accounts of 'flying' witches!
confusionNotes: The yellow flowers with purple veins are so distinctive that mature plants are hard to confuse with anything else. Young plants might be mistaken for other weedy nightshades, but the sticky, foul-smelling leaves are a dead giveaway - if it stinks, step back and don't touch!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'black henbane,' the flowers are actually yellow - the 'black' refers to the dark seeds. This plant is extremely toxic to humans and animals, containing dangerous alkaloids that can cause hallucinations, convulsions, and death. Never handle without gloves and keep children and pets away.
compareHints: Black henbane is the only Hyoscyamus species in New England, making it unique among our nightshades. Unlike other members of the nightshade family such as horse nettle or bittersweet, henbane's flowers have those telltale dark purple veins on yellow petals. Most other nightshades in our region have solid-colored purple, white, or yellow flowers without the intricate vein patterns.
